title: By the River
focus: despair and renewal by the river

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha reaches the river and, sick of himself, leans to drown. From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience despair to learn its emptiness, and decides to stay by the river.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Now, Siddhartha smiled” slowly and put it in my own words: Govinda, now a monk, has watched over a sleeping stranger and does not recognize him; when he asks how the stranger knows his name, Siddhartha smiles. Next, craft. I notice the line is only four words, set alone after the monk's puzzled question, so the smile answers him before any words do. The strongest word is “smiled”: the smile is the first calm, knowing gesture after his despair at the river, so it marks a man who has come back to himself. Then, effect. Why does Siddhartha smile when the monk asks how he knows his name? My answer: The monk is his old friend Govinda, who cannot recognize him; Siddhartha smiles because he has just woken by the river calm and renewed, no longer the weary rich merchant who came to the river in despair.

contentNotes.teacherNote: At the river Siddhartha intends to end his life. Use the safe-messaging script; the quiz item asks what his despair leads him toward. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…ly was a tiger to devour him! If there only was a wine, a poison which would numb his senses,…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
